column2: The righteous creature is honoured everywhere, without doubt. "Go by your own merits to my abode, endowed with every enjoyment.
If there is any wrongdoing left, you will enjoy its fruit later, right here." Thus Yama, honouring him and sending him to a good state,
summons sinners and threatens them with the staff of Time. His voice is like the roar of the clouds of dissolution; he is dark as a collyrium mountain,
flashing like lightning, terrible, fearsome, with thirty-two arms, three yojanas broad, red-eyed, long-nosed,
with a face made fearful by tusks, and eyes fierce as wells; joined by Death-fever and the rest. Chitragupta too is terrifying.
All the messengers roar, as fearsome as Yama. Then to all the trembling sinners
who grieve over their deeds, Chitragupta speaks by Yama's command: "O wicked sinners, of bad conduct, corrupted by pride,
why did you, without discernment, earn sin, seen with desire, anger and the rest, with a proud mind?
Whatever was the more sinful, why did you do that, people? You did those sins before with great delight.
So now you must experience the torments; why in vain are you so miserable? As you did evil for servants, friends and wives,
so by the force of your karma you have reached here, in great misery. The sons and others you nourished have gone elsewhere;
that sin has come to you alone; why the cause of grief? As you did many sins,
so you have received sufferings; why are you grieving here? Reflect on what you did before.
'Yama will inflict punishment' — did you not think of this? Whether poor or foolish, learned or wealthy,
a coward or a hero, Yama is held to be impartial." Hearing Chitragupta's words, the sinners then
grieving over their deeds, stay silent, terrified. The cruel, fierce, fearsome messengers who carry out Yama's orders,
Chanda and others, forcibly hurl them into the hells. Having enjoyed the fruit of their evil deeds, at the end, with the remainder of sin,
they reach the earth and become immovable things and the like. Narada said: "Lord, a doubt has arisen in my mind, O ocean of compassion;
you are able to cut it, for you are our elder. Various dharmas have been taught, and many sins as well.
You, knowing much, have said their fruit is enjoyed for a long time. At the end of Brahma's day, destruction of the three worlds is declared;
at the end of two parardhas, the destruction of the cosmic egg too. Of the merit of gifts of villages and the like, you yourself, son of Brahma,
have said the great enjoyment lasts for a thousand crores of kalpas. At the natural dissolution all worlds are destroyed.
You said that only one remains, Janardana. This is my doubt; may you resolve it:
for the enjoyments of merit and sin, in the flood of dissolution, is there no completion?" Sanaka said: "Well asked, O greatly wise one; this is the most secret of secrets.
I shall tell you what you ask; listen with attention. Narayana is imperishable, infinite, the supreme eternal light,
pure, without qualities, eternal, free of the delusion of maya; though without qualities, he shines as supreme bliss as if with qualities,
and appears as if divided into Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva and the rest. In these three, divided by the limiting adjunct of qualities, O eternal one,
uniting maya he does the work of the whole world: in the form of Brahma he creates, in the form of Vishnu he protects,
and at the end, in the form of Rudra, he devours all — this is certain. At the end of dissolution Janardana arises in Brahma's form
and fashions the universe, moving and unmoving, as before. Whatever the immovable and others were and wherever they were placed, O best of Brahmins,
Brahma makes the whole world as before. Therefore of sins and merits done, O best,
the imperishable fruit of actions must be enjoyed without fail. Karma is not exhausted unenjoyed even in hundreds of crores of kalpas.
Action done, good or bad, must certainly be enjoyed. The God who is the inner Self of all worlds, the world's essence, full and eternal, enjoys the fruit of all actions.
That God who supports the universe, established in the distinction of qualities, creates, protects and devours all this; he is all-enjoying and imperishable."
One pure, imperishable, eternal Supreme Self, the substance of the world, appears divided in men by differences of understanding.
The one without a second is the supreme Brahman, eternal, sung by the Vedanta; therefore there is nothing higher, O Brahmin.
The Supreme Self without qualities has no action or duty, form or colour, doer-hood or enjoyer-hood.
The ground of all causes, the light beyond lights, beyond which there is nothing else — that is to be known for liberation.
What is made of the Word-Brahman, the great sayings and the rest — knowledge born of reflecting on them is the highest means of liberation.
For those without right knowledge the world appears manifold; for the supremely wise, this is all of the nature of Supreme Brahman.
The one, supreme bliss, without qualities, higher than the highest, imperishable, appears bearing many forms by difference of understanding.
Those under maya see difference in the Supreme Self by maya; therefore the seeker of liberation should give up maya through yoga.
Maya is neither of the nature of being nor non-being, nor both; it is to be known as indescribable, giver of the notion of difference.
Maya itself is understood by the word "ignorance"; thus for those who have conquered maya there is the cutting of ignorance.
The eternal Supreme Brahman is called by the word "knowledge"; to the knowers the Supreme Self shines constantly in the heart.
The yogi destroys ignorance by yoga, O best of sages. Yoga is accomplished by eight limbs; I shall tell them truly.
Yamas and niyamas, postures, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana,
and samadhi — these are the limbs of yoga in order, O best of sages. I shall tell their characteristics in brief.
Non-violence, truth, non-stealing, celibacy, non-possession, freedom from anger and from envy are briefly declared as the yamas.
That which causes no pain to any beings is called non-violence by the good, and gives success in yoga.
Speaking in accordance with fact, with discrimination between dharma and adharma, they call truth. Now hear non-stealing.
The taking of another's property by theft or force is called stealing by the good; non-stealing is its opposite.
Renunciation of sexual union everywhere is declared celibacy. Through abandoning celibacy, even a learned man becomes a sinner.
One who has renounced all attachment but engages in sexual union is to be known as equal to a Chandala, cast out from all classes.
A person devoted to yoga who longs for sense-objects — merely by speaking with him, men incur the guilt of Brahmin-slaying.
If one who has renounced all attachment becomes attached again, those who associate with his company share the fault of great sin.
Not taking property even in distress, O lord of sages, is called non-possession, which brings accomplishment of yoga.
Harsh speech out of self-exaltation they call anger — the knowers of dharma; non-anger is its opposite.
Great mental burning on seeing another richer in wealth and the like is declared by the good as envy; giving it up is freedom from envy.
Thus in brief the yamas have been told, O best of the wise. I shall also tell you the niyamas; hear them, Narada.
Austerity, study, contentment, purity, worship of Hari, and chiefly the twilight worship are declared the niyamas.
Where there is drying up of the body by the Chandrayana and the like, that is called austerity by the good, the best means to yoga.
Chanting Om, the Upanishads, the twelve-syllable and eight-syllable mantras and the group of great sayings, O Brahmin,
is called study and is the best means to yoga. The fool who gives up study does not succeed in yoga.
Even without yoga, by study men's sins are destroyed; and the gods, pleased by study, become gracious.
Chanting is said to be threefold: spoken, whispered and mental. Among the three, each earlier is lower than the later, O best of Brahmins.
Properly pronouncing the mantra with clear syllables and words is called spoken chanting, giving the fruit of all sacrifices.
Pronouncing the mantra with some separation of word from word is called whispered chanting, twice better than the former.
Arranging the syllables in a row and reflecting on their meaning is called mental chanting, which gives success in yoga.
By chanting, the god is pleased with one who constantly praises; therefore one endowed with study obtains all desires.
Satisfaction with what comes by chance is called contentment. A man without contentment finds happiness nowhere.
Desire is never quieted by the enjoyment of desires; "When shall I get more than this?" — thus desire increases.
Therefore, giving up desire, which dries up the body, one should be content with what comes by chance and devoted to dharma.
Purity is held to be twofold, outer and inner: outer purity is by earth and water; inner is purity of feeling.
The various sacrifices performed by those lacking inner purity bear no fruit, O best of sages, like oblations put into ashes.
For those lacking purity of feeling all action is fruitless; therefore, abandoning passion and the rest, one should be happy.
Even one who has purified himself with thousands of loads of clay and ten million jars of water, if wicked in mind, is held to be like a Chandala.
If one lacking inner purity is devoted to worship of gods, that very god destroys him and he falls into hell.
One lacking inner purity who practises outer purity, like a decorated liquor-jar, does not attain peace.
Rivers do not purify those without purity of mind who go on pilgrimage, any more than a liquor-jar.
One who speaks dharma with his speech but desires sin in mind should be known as the foremost of great sinners.
Those of pure mind who do even only the highest dharma — know their fruit to be imperishable and happiness-giving.
He whose devotion to Hari is firm in deed, mind and word, by praise, hearing and worship, is said to perform "worship of Hari".
The yamas and niyamas have been taught in brief; for those of pure mind they know liberation to be in hand.
With the yamas and niyamas, the steady-minded, master of senses should well practise posture, the best means to yoga.
Lotus, svastika, pitha, lion, cock, elephant, tortoise, thunderbolt (vajra), boar, deer and cloth postures;
heron, tube, all-auspicious, bull, serpent, fish, tiger and half-moon;
staff, wind, mountain, sky, mudga, crocodile, three-path, wood, post, and "vaikarnika";
earth and hero postures — causes for accomplishing yoga. Thirty postures have been taught by the great sages.
Having taken up one of these, devoted to the teacher, the practitioner should conquer the breaths, beyond dualities and free of envy.
Facing east, north or west, in a silent place without people, he should conquer breath by practice.
Prana is the wind in the body; its control is "ayama"; thus it is called pranayama, declared twofold.
It is "agarbha" and "sagarbha"; the second is the better of the two. Without chanting and meditation it is agarbha; with them, sagarbha.
Exhalation, inhalation, retention and emptiness: thus pranayama is declared fourfold by the wise.
In creatures the right channel is called pingala, presided over by the sun, and heard to be the womb of the ancestors.
The left channel is known as ida, the womb of the gods; know the moon as its presiding deity, O best of sages.
Between these two lies the channel called sushumna, very subtle, most secret, to be known as presided over by Brahma.
He should exhale the wind through the left; from exhaling it is "rechaka". He should inhale through the right; from filling it is "puraka".
Holding the wind filling his body and not releasing it, remaining like a full jar — that is the famed "kumbhaka".
Neither taking in nor letting out the wind, staying inside and outside — know that as the pranayama called "shunyaka" (void).
Breath must be conquered slowly, like a mad elephant; otherwise dreadful great diseases arise.
The yogi, free of sin, should join the wind gradually; freed from all sins, he attains Brahma's abode.
Drawing back all the senses attached to sense-objects, the lord of sages restrains them — this is called "pratyahara".
Great souls with conquered senses, even without meditation, go to the Supreme Brahman, from which return is hard.
One who is devoted to meditation without having conquered the host of senses is to be known as of deluded mind, and his meditation does not succeed.
Whatever he sees, he should see all as like the self in the self; holding the withdrawn senses is "dharana".
Through yoga, with the host of senses conquered, he should firmly draw them in the heart and meditate on the Supreme Self, the sustainer of all, Achyuta.
Vishnu, the Self of the whole universe, the single cause of all, with eyes like open lotus petals, adorned with lovely earrings,
long-armed, of noble limbs, adorned with all ornaments, wearing yellow garments, with a golden sacred thread,
bearing a garland of tulsi, shining with the Kaustubha, with the Shrivatsa on his chest, saluted by gods and demons —
in the heart-lotus of eight spokes, twelve finger-breadths wide, he should meditate on the unmanifest Self, the all-pervading, higher than the highest.
Meditation is declared by the good as one-pointedness of cognition. Having meditated even for a moment, a man gains supreme liberation.
By meditation sins are destroyed; by meditation one gains liberation; by meditation Hari is pleased; meditation accomplishes all aims.
Whatever form of Mahavishnu he wishes, he should meditate on attentively; pleased by that meditation, Hari gives liberation.
He should make the mind steady on the object of meditation, O best, so that meditation, the object and the meditator disappear utterly.
Then immortality arises through partaking of the nectar of knowledge; through constant meditation, non-difference is established.
Joined with supreme bliss as in deep sleep, senses stilled, steady like a lamp in a windless place, he is said to be in samadhi.
In the state of samadhi the yogi neither hears, sees, smells, touches, nor speaks anything, O best.
The Self is stainless, pure, of the form of being-consciousness-bliss, free of all limiting adjuncts, and shines steadily to yogis.
The Supreme God, though without qualities, seems through ignorance to have qualities; when ignorance is destroyed, he shines as he stood before.
The supreme light, of immeasurable nature, seems to possess maya for those under maya; at its destruction it reveals the stainless Brahman to the wise.
One without a second, the supreme light, taintless, stands as the inner controller of all beings.
Subtler than the subtle, greater than the great, the eternal Self, cause of the whole universe — the best of the knowers see him, the highest of the highest, the supreme purifier.
He who stands in the differences of letters from "a" to "ksha", the ancient Person, beginningless, is sung as the Word-Brahman.
Pure, imperishable, eternal, full, in the midst of space, bliss, stainless, peaceful — he is sung as the Supreme Brahman.
Yogis see in the heart the eternal Supreme Self, changeless, unborn, pure, who is sung as the Supreme Brahman.
I shall tell another meditation; hear, O best of sages — like a rain of nectar for men scorched by the heat of samsara.
He should remember Narayana, supreme bliss, abiding in Om, of the form of sound, incomparable, standing above the half-measure.
A is Brahma's form, "u" is like Vishnu's form, "m" is Rudra's form, and the half-measure is the Supreme Self.
The three measures are said to be presided over by Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva; their combination, O Brahmin, awakens to the Supreme Brahman.
The Supreme Brahman is what is denoted, and Om is the denoter; the relation of denoted and denoter is, O Brahmins, figurative.
Those who constantly chant Om are freed from all sins; joined with its practice they gain supreme liberation.
Chanting the Om mantra, whose nature is Brahma, Vishnu and Shiva, he should meditate within on a stainless splendour like ten million suns.
Or in the form of the Shaligrama stone or an image, or whatever sin-removing object, he should contemplate in the heart.
This Vaishnava knowledge, which has been told to you, O lord of sages — knowing this the best of yogis gains supreme liberation.
Whoever attentively hears or reads this is freed from all sins and attains Hari's world (salokya).
After ten million thousand births in immovable forms and the like, to one wandering, a human birth is somehow obtained.
Even there, O best, the idea of the divine, of giving, and of enjoyment in men is the fruit of austerity from other births.
Having obtained a rare human birth, one who does not worship Hari even once — who is a greater fool than he, dull-witted and unconscious?
Those who, having got a human birth so hard to get, do not worship Hari — where does the discrimination of such utter fools stand?
Worshipped, the Lord of the world grants the desired fruit. Who, burned by samsara, would not worship him, O Brahmin?
Even a Chandala who is a devotee of Vishnu is above a Brahmin, O best of sages; and a Brahmin without devotion to Vishnu is lower than a dog-cooker.
Therefore, abandoning desire and the like, one should worship the imperishable Hari, by whose pleasing all is pleased, since Hari is all-pervading.
As in an elephant's footprint all footprints are absorbed, so the moving and unmoving universe is absorbed in Vishnu.
As the world, moving and unmoving, is pervaded by space, so this whole moving and unmoving universe is pervaded by Hari.
Death follows birth for men, and birth is the means to death; know both are near. Their destruction is by serving Hari.
Meditated on, remembered, worshipped or bowed to, who would not worship Janardana, cutter of the noose of samsara?
By merely uttering whose name great sins are destroyed, and by worshipping whom, O Brahmin sage, a man becomes a sharer in liberation —
Ah, wonder! Ah, wonder! Ah, wonder, O Brahmin: while Hari's name exists, people still whirl in samsara!
I shall say it again and again, O rich in austerity, and it is true: led by Yama's soldiers, powerless by means of dharma...
